title: Fenerbahce v Liverpool: Where to Watch, Kick Off Time & More - roundtable.io
content: A tricky away test for Liverpool in Europe as they travel to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce in an intriguing clash for Andoni Iraola's men. The Reds go into this game off the back of a frustrating defeat at home to Arsenal as the Merseyside club's momentum was halted by a stubborn Gunners outfit. As for Fenerbahce, they have recently sacked their manager, Ismail Kartal and have replaced him, in the interim, with former LFC player Dirk Kuyt, with his one and only game ending in a loss in the league. Liverpool will be looking to bounce back from a narrow loss to the reigning Premier League champions over the weekend. Kai Havertz was the one who scored the all-important goal for the Gunners following a misplaced pass from Alisson Becker, which was capitalised on by a Declan Rice run around the outside of the LFC defence. He played a ball across the six yard and Havertz tapped it into an open net. Despite Andoni Iraola's side pushing and probing, they couldn't find the clinical final touch to break past David Raya, and it left many at Anfield with mixed feelings as they left the stadium. On the one hand, Liverpool played well and dominated the game for at least 60 of the 90 minutes, but on the other hand, they failed to register a shot on target and looked toothless in attack. The hosts for this game go into it desperate to try and find some form, given their poor start to the campaign both domestically and in Europe. In the league, they sit sixth after 10 games, with there being a nine point gap between them and the league leaders Galatasaray. And in the Champions League it hasn't been much better, with Fenerbahce having just two points from their first three games. They have drawn against Roma and Slavia Prague, but were humiliated by Aston Villa, losing 6-0 at Villa Park. Despite the poor form, they still possess several players who could cause the Reds problems on the night. The likes of Romelu Lukaku, ex-Man City goalkeeper Ederson and World Cup winner N'Golo Kante are all in the Fenerbahce squad, and have the ability to be gamechangers for the 19- time Turkish Super Lig champions. The game will be played on Wednesday 4th November 2026, and kicks off at 5:45 pm. In the UK, you can watch the game live on TNT Sports/HBO Max. In the US, you can watch the game live on Paramount+. In Australia, you can watch the game live on Stan Sport. Comment Below: Where In The World Will You Be Watching This Game From?

Skyler Gisondo is set to star in the series as Jimmy Olsen, reprising his role from 2025's Superman. He revealed in a recent interview that the project is now one step closer to finishing production. As revealed by Gisondo to Collider, filming has wrapped up on the mockumentary. The show will see Jimmy Olsen host a true-crime docuseries to investigate whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongfully convicted of murdering his father, the king of Gorilla City. Gorilla Grodd was first introduced as a Flash villain in the comics, which has fans speculating that the character might have a cameo set in the DCU already. While nowhere as wacky as characters like Mister Mxyzptlk or Mister Mind, Gorilla Grodd would still give the average mainstream audience some pause for thought. Gorilla Grodd was created by John Broome and Carmine Infantino and first appeared in the comics in The Flash #106 in May 1959. He belongs to a city of intelligent gorillas and stands out as a single evil gorilla in an otherwise peaceful society. Grodd also gained mental powers after he was exposed to the radiation of a meteorite. While usually serving as a Flash villain, Gorilla Grodd has butted heads with the likes of the Justice League, Superman, and Batman. He has been on supervillain teams like the Injustice League and the Legion of Doom. The character has featured in some of the most popular DC adaptations, such as CW's Arrowverse and Injustice 2. title: Substantiation and Professional Reliance Failures in Closely Held C Corporations: An Analysis of Glass Warehouse, LLC v. Commissioner - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Glass Warehouse, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-111, November 2, 2026 For tax practitioners advising closely held corporate clients, Glass Warehouse, LLC v. Commissioner serves as a stark reminder of the foundational evidentiary burdens required under the Internal Revenue Code. The decision underscores two key operational lessons for certified public accountants and enrolled agents: first, reporting shareholder payments on Form 1040 as “other income” does not satisfy the corporation’s statutory obligation under Section 162 and Section 6001 to substantiate trade or business expenses; and second, invoking a defense of reasonable cause based on professional tax reliance under Section 6664(c) requires concrete affirmative evidence of communication, full disclosure, and actual advice, rather than mere assertions that a return was prepared by an external CPA. Glass Warehouse, LLC (petitioner) operated as a closely held C corporation principally located in San Diego, California, with additional inventory warehouses in California and Texas. The corporation specialized in selling glass shower doors and enclosures through major online retail platforms, including Home Depot, Wayfair, and Houzz, generating annual gross receipts of approximately $4.1 million for the tax year ending June 30, 2019. During the tax years at issue (ending June 30, 2018, and June 30, 2019), the petitioner was owned and managed by two shareholder-officers: Ryan Thatcher, who served as president and held an 80% ownership interest, and Nidal Hanna, who served as vice president and held a 20% ownership interest. Mr. Thatcher and Ms. Hanna were married during the relevant period and worked full time for the corporation, managing all day-to-day operations including sales, inventory purchasing, employee supervision, and customer acquisition. The corporation employed approximately ten employees, including an accounting manager, Mallory Copeland, who managed payroll, accounts payable, and accounts receivable using QuickBooks software, from which data was exported to Microsoft Excel spreadsheets. The petitioner retained an external CPA firm, Ahuja & Clark, PLLC, which was provided access to the corporation’s QuickBooks accounting files. For the tax year ending June 30, 2019, petitioner filed Form 1120 (U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return), reporting $71,250 in officer compensation on Line 12 ($35,625 allocated each to Mr. Thatcher and Ms. Hanna on Form 1125-E). On Form W-2 (Wage and Tax Statement), petitioner reported officer wages of $92,712 for Mr. Thatcher and $73,962 for Ms. Hanna. In addition, petitioner claimed a corporate deduction of $173,974 for “subcontractor fees” on Form 1120. This total included $109,819 purportedly paid to its two shareholder-officers ($98,774 to Mr. Thatcher and $11,045 to Ms. Hanna). Petitioner did not issue Form 1099-MISC or Form 1099-NEC to either shareholder-officer for 2019. On their joint individual income tax return (Form 1040) for 2019, Mr. Thatcher and Ms. Hanna reported $166,674 in aggregate Form W-2 wages and reported the $109,819 in purported subcontractor payments as “Other income,” remitting self-employment/employment taxes thereon. On August 18, 2022, the Internal Revenue Service issued a Notice of Deficiency determining: In the Notice of Deficiency, respondent disallowed $118,302 of petitioner’s claimed $173,974 subcontractor expense deduction for tax year 2019 for lack of substantiation. Petitioner filed a timely petition with the United States Tax Court on November 9, 2022. Prior to trial, the parties executed a Stipulation of Settled Issues resolving all adjustments for tax year 2018 except petitioner’s liability for the Section 6662(a) penalty, while respondent conceded the Section 6662(a) penalty for tax year 2019. Before the Tax Court, petitioner requested relief on two remaining contested issues: To support its deduction claim, petitioner asserted that the subcontractor payments were substantiated by the trial testimony of its accounting manager, corporate accounting records, and the joint Form 1040 of the shareholder-officers. Petitioner further argued that the reporting arrangement reflected worker misclassification, for which Section 3509 provided a legal framework protecting against treasury loss. With respect to penalty relief, petitioner argued that it exercised ordinary business care by retaining a qualified external CPA firm whose signature appeared on the corporate returns. Judge Fung structured the Tax Court’s analysis around well-established statutory provisions and judicial precedents governing corporate tax deductions and penalty compliance. Under Rule 142(a) of the Tax Court Rules of Practice and Procedure and the seminal doctrine of Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933), the Commissioner’s determinations in a Notice of Deficiency are presumed correct, and the taxpayer carries the burden of proving them erroneous. While Section 7491(a) permits a shift in the burden of proof to the Commissioner under specific conditions, the court emphasized that this statutory shift “applies, however, only if the taxpayer complies with all substantiation and recordkeeping requirements under the Code.” The court highlighted the foundational principle that tax deductions are strictly a “matter of legislative grace, and taxpayers bear the burden of proving entitlement to each deduction claimed” (INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992)). Meeting this standard requires taxpayers to demonstrate compliance with statutory authorization and Section 6001 recordkeeping obligations (Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a)). Specifically, the court affirmed that “[a]dequate substantiation must establish the nature, amount, and purpose of a claimed deduction” (Higbee v. Commissioner, 116 T.C. 438, 440 (2001)). Where evidentiary gaps persist, “we must sustain the Commissioner’s determination and disallow the deduction” (Rogers v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-141). Section 162(a)(1) permits a business deduction for ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the tax year, including a “reasonable allowance for salaries or other compensation for personal services actually rendered.” Interpreting this provision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit—to which an appeal in this case would lie pursuant to Section 7482(b)(1)(B)—applies a two-prong test: Because the Commissioner conceded the reasonableness of the overall compensation and disallowed the deduction solely for lack of substantiation, the court observed that it was unnecessary to resolve whether the payments carried compensatory intent or represented disguised dividends. In applying the legal framework to the record, the court determined that petitioner failed to meet even minimum substantiation thresholds. Petitioner relied heavily on the testimony of its accounting manager, Ms. Copeland. However, the court found that Ms. Copeland’s testimony described only the shareholder-officers’ ordinary, day-to-day executive duties—managing sales, inventory, personnel, and customer relations. The court noted: “Ms. Copeland’s only testimony describing Mr. Thatcher’s services concerned his day-to-day work for the petitioner—‘manag[ing] every aspect of the company, customers, inventory buying, all of it’—including managing employees and ‘responsibility for attracting or retaining customers.’ She similarly did not offer any specific information about services provided by Ms. Hanna. And Ms. Copeland testified that she did not see Mr. Thatcher or Ms. Hanna involved in the business in any capacity beyond their day-to-day operations work.” The court observed that while a corporation is free to structure separate subcontractor arrangements with its officers under Gregory v. Helvering, 293 U.S. 465, 469 (1935), and Menard, Inc. v. Commissioner, 560 F.3d 620, 623 (7th Cir. 2009), “[t]he record does not contain any documents or any testimony showing that such an arrangement existed.” Petitioner failed to present written subcontractor contracts, invoices, project logs, or Forms 1099. In contrast, Ms. Copeland acknowledged issuing Forms 1099 to other third-party workers whose specific subcontracted tasks she personally knew. The court firmly rejected petitioner’s argument that reporting $109,819 as “Other income” on the shareholders’ personal Form 1040 substantiated the corporate deduction: “How a shareholder reports an item on a personal tax return does not control how the corporation reports that same item on its own tax return because a corporation is generally recognized as a tax entity separate from its shareholders.” (Moline Props., Inc. v. Commissioner, 319 U.S. 436, 438–39 (1943)). Quoting Higgins v. Smith, 308 U.S. 473, 477 (1940), the court stressed that “[a] taxpayer is free to adopt [any] organization for his affairs as he may choose and having elected to do some business as a corporation, he must accept the tax disadvantages.” The court also dismissed petitioner’s reliance on Section 3509 worker misclassification relief, emphasizing: “Section 3509 does not turn amounts that would otherwise not be subject to withholding tax, such as contractor expenses, into deductible Form W–2 wages just because the Code provides a mechanism to hold an employer liable in an actual worker misclassification situation.” Because petitioner offered no factual evidence of misclassification or underlying contract work, the $118,302 disallowance was sustained in full. The remaining controversy centered on the 20% accuracy-related penalty imposed under Section 6662(a) for tax year 2018. Under Section 6662(b)(2) and Section 6662(d)(1)(B), a substantial understatement of income tax for a subchapter C corporation occurs if the understatement exceeds the lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return (or, if greater, $10,000) or $10,000,000. For 2018, petitioner reported tax of $92,775, whereas the tax required to be shown was $107,775, resulting in a substantial understatement under the statute. Significantly, the court clarified the statutory burden of proof rules under Section 7491(c). While the Commissioner holds the burden of production regarding penalties for individual taxpayers, Section 7491(c) “applies only to individuals, not corporations, so respondent bears no burden of production here” (NT, Inc. v. Commissioner, 126 T.C. 191, 195 (2006)). Consequently, petitioner carried the burden of establishing an affirmative defense under Section 6664(c). (The court confirmed IRS compliance with Section 6751(b) written supervisory approval requirements through Exhibit 4-J, noting under Laidlaw’s Harley Davidson Sales, Inc. v. Commissioner, 29 F.4th 1066, 1074 (9th Cir. 2022), that written approval was timely executed prior to notice issuance). To establish the affirmative defense of reasonable cause and good faith under Section 6664(c)(1), a taxpayer must demonstrate that it “exercised ordinary business care and prudence as to the disputed item” (Neonatology Assocs., P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43, 98 (2000)). Under Neonatology Associates, reasonable reliance on a professional tax advisor requires satisfying three specific evidentiary elements: The court found petitioner’s defense entirely unbefitting these requirements: “The record is devoid of any testimony or other evidence of any information petitioner provided to an adviser regarding its tax position. At trial petitioner introduced no evidence showing that it sought or received any advice from Ahuja & Clark, the paid preparer identified on petitioner’s return... No witness testified about any interaction with any return preparer regarding the preparation of, or the positions taken on, petitioner’s return.” Refusing to accept unsworn assertions by petitioner’s trial counsel, the court cited Rule 143(c) of the Tax Court Rules of Practice and Procedure and Niedringhaus v. Commissioner, 99 T.C. 202, 214 n.7 (1992), emphasizing that “[s]tatements in briefs . . . do not constitute evidence.” Holding petitioner liable for the Section 6662(a) penalty, Judge Fung concluded with a clear regulatory standard: “Simply hiring a tax preparer does not insulate a taxpayer from the consequences of the tax positions on its return.” (Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(b)(1)). The United States Tax Court concluded its analysis with two binding determinations: Copyright © 2025 Thomas, Zollars & Lynch, Ltd., All Rights Reserved

title: Honda CR-V Owners Named the Best Used Years, But the 2014 They Skipped Is the Newest One Without a CVT or Turbo - Torque News
content: A used car shopper asked Reddit for the best used Honda CR-V years without a CVT or a turbo, and CR-V owners praised the 2011 and the 2019 to 2022 models. But every CR-V from 2015 on uses a CVT, so the newest CR-V with neither is actually a 2014. The 2012 to 2014 CR-V pairs a 2.4-liter engine with a traditional five-speed automatic. Here is what owners said, what they missed, and why one 2011 owner faced an $8,000 transmission quote at 170,000 miles. Just because certain generations were rated highly doesn't mean individual examples have aged well. It will be hard to find a good early CR-V today, and a 15-year-old car only makes sense for specific needs and budgets. What Honda CR-V Owners Said About the Best Used Years It started with this question on Reddit. "Which years of Honda CR-V are the best? I want to avoid the CVT and turbo." Here is a sampling of the responses, edited as always for content, grammar, and clarity. The only top-level comment was also the most detailed, though it reads like a summary, so its claims are worth checking. Note that the commenter's 2016 pick uses a CVT, which this shopper wants to avoid. The same goes for every 2019 to 2022 CR-V. That comment drew several replies. "The LX versions of the early fifth generation came with the K24, not the 1.5 turbo, so they're worth a look, but they're very basic," one said. Another backed the 2011. "It really does feel like the one if you're avoiding both the turbo and the CVT, since that 2.4-liter with the traditional automatic keeps going with basic maintenance." The first commenter then shared their own experience. "Within the past week, I picked up a used 2020 CR-V Touring for my wife after a drunk driver totaled her car, and we went with a CR-V because she previously had one." "It was a 2011 CR-V, and the transmission died at about 170,000 miles, after about 12 years. We were quoted $8,000 for a replacement, or $6,000 with a 30-day warranty, so we just replaced the car." The Newest Used Honda CR-V Without a CVT or Turbo Is a 2014 Honda switched the CR-V to a CVT for 2015, and every gas CR-V since has used one. That makes the 2012 to 2014 models, with their 2.4-liter engine and five-speed automatic, the newest CR-Vs that meet this shopper's rules. Here is how the generations break down for anyone shopping the best used Honda CR-V years. The CR-V Hybrid Is Another Way Around the CVT and Turbo The 2020 and newer CR-V Hybrid uses Honda's two-motor system, with no turbo and no conventional belt-driven CVT. It also brings strong fuel economy, and owners say the CR-V Hybrid hits 43 mpg if you drive it right. Shoppers should know Honda extended head gasket coverage to 10 years or 150,000 miles on 2020 to 2026 CR-V Hybrids and on turbo CR-Vs. On a used example, that coverage counts from the original sale date, so check how much time is left. Some owners already plan around that clock. Take the CR-V Hybrid owner who plans to sell at 10 years over the head gasket. If you want a used CR-V without a CVT or turbo, a 2012 to 2014 model is the newest and easiest to find in good shape. A 2011 can still work, but finding a clean 15-year-old example takes patience. If you can live with a CVT, a 2019 to 2022 model adds modern features like Apple CarPlay. Either way, get a pre-purchase inspection and a full service history. Fuel economy matters more for drivers who rack up miles. That came up when CR-V owners told a buyer who commutes 14 times a week the good and the bad. Some CR-V owners still cross-shop Toyota. Take one 2025 CR-V owner who drove a 2026 RAV4 450 miles and still refused to buy one. Shoppers who would rather buy new can also wait for the all-new 2028 Honda CR-V. Reports suggest Honda may make the CR-V hybrid only. Would you buy a 2014 CR-V to avoid the CVT and turbo, or does a newer model's tech win out? title: No Release, But a Five-Year Stay: Protecting the Non-Debtor Principal After Purdue - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. In Harrington v. Purdue Pharma L.P., the Supreme Court issued its landmark ruling holding that “the bankruptcy code does not authorize a release and injunction that, as part of a plan of reorganization under Chapter 11, effectively seeks to discharge claims against a nondebtor without the consent of affected claimants.” 603 U.S. 204, 227 (2024). Since its ruling, bankruptcy courts have had to grapple with questions left unanswered by the Supreme Court’s ruling. In this post, we examine one of those unanswered questions: whether as part of a plan of reorganization under subchapter V, the court may issue an injunction protecting a non-debtor for the life of the plan. The Second Circuit has held that in limited circumstances the automatic stay may be extended to non-debtors “when a claim against the non-debtor will have an immediate adverse economic consequence for the debtor’s estate.” Queenie, Ltd. v. Nygard Int’l, 321 F.3d 282, 287 (2d Cir. 2003). This includes situations where “there is such identity between the debtor and the third-party defendant that the debtor may be said to be the real party defendant.” Id. at 288 (quoting A.H. Robins Co. v. Piccinin, 788 F.2d 994, 999 (4th Cir. 1986)). In In re Hal Luftig Co., Hal Luftig Company, Inc. (the “Debtor”) was a theatrical production company that developed, acquired, and promoted theatrical plays, musicals, and similar works. No. 25-CV-02580 (MMG), 2026 WL 2935950, at *1 (S.D.N.Y. Sept. 30, 2026). Hal Luftig (“Mr. Luftig”) was the president and sole shareholder of the Debtor. A former business partner of the Debtor (the “Creditor”) obtained a $2.6 million arbitration award, later confirmed and reduced to judgment, against the Debtor and Mr. Luftig jointly and severally. At the outset of the case, the Debtor obtained an extension of the automatic stay to Mr. Luftig, arguing that the Debtor derived profits from shows produced by Mr. Luftig and his ability to produce these shows would be frustrated if he had to deal with enforcement actions from the Creditor. After the district court declined to adopt the bankruptcy court’s proposed findings and denied confirmation of an initial plan containing a non-debtor third party release, In re Hal Luftig Co., 657 B.R. 704 (S.D.N.Y. 2024), the Debtor proposed a plan that continued the automatic stay protecting Mr. Luftig for the life of the five-year plan. The bankruptcy court confirmed the plan, finding that the extension of the automatic stay was necessary to facilitate an effective reorganization. In re Hal Luftig Co., 667 B.R. 638, 659–62 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. 2025). On appeal, a principal argument raised by the Creditor was that an extension of the stay for the life of the plan was impermissible under Purdue Pharma because it effectively operated as a discharge of a non-debtor third party for the life of the plan. Here the district court carefully distinguished the difference between the relief being requested and the discharge in Purdue Pharma, providing that “[t]he discharge at issue in Harrington was a permanent extinguishing of non-debtor liabilities without the consent of the affected creditors, and without subjecting the released parties to the bankruptcy process. A time-limited pause on enforcement or collection actions, through an automatic stay extension, is fundamentally different, and much closer to the ordinary and commonplace powers afforded to bankruptcy courts to effectuate debtor reorganizations.” In re Hal Luftig Co., 2026 WL 2935950, at *4 (citation omitted). Accordingly, the district court affirmed the bankruptcy court’s order confirming the plan. However, the court cautioned that its decision was confined to the facts and record of the case, and that a stay over a plan of substantially longer duration, or under different facts, might amount to “the functional equivalent of an impermissible discharge of a non-debtor.” Id. at *5. Read alongside Judge McMahon’s observation on the Purdue remand that Harrington “left unchanged” a bankruptcy court’s power to temporarily enjoin litigation against third parties whose assets or claims could affect the estate, In re Purdue Pharma L.P., No. 24-Civ-7042, 2024 WL 4894349, at *7 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 26, 2024), and Judge Glenn’s confirmation of a Subchapter V plan with a five-year principal injunction over the U.S. Trustee’s objection, In re Fortuna Auction LLC, No. 25-10632 (MG), 2025 WL 3726083, at *18 (Bankr. S.D.N.Y. Dec. 19, 2025), Hal Luftig confirms that the post-Harrington tool for protecting a principal is a section 105 injunction supported by findings, not a plan release. For Subchapter V debtors whose principal shares joint-and-several liability with the company: debtors should file the stay-extension adversary on the petition date, build the record on why the principal is operationally indispensable, and carry the injunction into the plan by its terms rather than asking for anything that resembles a release. title: V. Joyce Cheek - West Bend News
content: Northwest Ohio and Northeast Indiana Local News Northwest Ohio and Northeast Indiana Local News V. Joyce Cheek, 95, of Antwerp, passed away Thursday, October 29, 2026 at her home. Joyce was born in Fort Wayne on March 8, 1931, the daughter of the late Leona & Earl Shuherk. On September 28, 1968, Joyce married the love of her life, James (Jim) Cheek, and together they shared many wonderful and happy years. Joyce and Jim were actively involved in the American Legion and helped get it started at the Roller Rink in town. Joyce loved having her family gathered together at the cottage on Snow Lake. She also cherished her trips to Canada to visit her family and traveling out west to spend time with Jim’s family. Joyce was a kind, pleasant, and caring person who always had a warm smile and treated everyone she met with kindness. She will be remembered for her love of family, her warm heart, and the many special memories she created with those around her. Joyce will be sadly missed by her children, Rose (Rudy) Ouellette-French & Steve (Janice) Ouellette; grandchildren, Joseph & James; & great granddaughter, Aleea Rose French. She was preceded in death by her husband, Jim on April 25, 2017. Service is Thursday, November 5th at 10:30 AM with viewing one hour prior at Dooley Funeral Home, Antwerp. She will be laid to rest in Maumee Cemetery, Antwerp. In lieu of flowers, please make donations to Visiting Angels, 121 S. Walnut Street, Van Wert, Ohio 45891. content:
We provide legal, research, policy, and communications support to the state officials who protect our free and fair elections. We work with state officials to defend the Constitution, the authority of states to govern and serve their constituents, and our system of checks and balances. We work with law enforcement leaders, as well as state and local officials, in their efforts to keep elections safe, defend the rule of law, and strengthen community trust. We share the facts about our democracy and elections. And we help state officials ensure that voters have access to accurate information. We provide legal, research, policy, and communications support to the state officials who protect our free and fair elections. We work with state officials to defend the Constitution, the authority of states to govern and serve their constituents, and our system of checks and balances. We work with law enforcement leaders, as well as state and local officials, in their efforts to keep elections safe, defend the rule of law, and strengthen community trust. We share the facts about our democracy and elections. And we help state officials ensure that voters have access to accurate information. In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration repeatedly attempted to assert authority over state-run elections. With Election Day approaching, the administration turned its attention to election officials, asking them to implement its desired procedures and threatening them with prosecution if they refused. In October, the U.S. Department of Justice sued California election officials, seeking to force them to set aside tens of thousands of ballots based on unfounded allegations that thousands of noncitizens were registered to vote. Days later, the administration made similar allegations against Washington state. Federal officials threatened to prosecute individual election officials who refused to comply with their demands. On Oct. 29, a group of labor unions and nonprofit organizations sued the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, asking a federal judge to order a stop to the administration’s threats. The lawsuit argued that the Constitution gives states—not the president—the authority to administer elections and that the Justice Department’s demands amounted to unlawful intimidation under federal voting rights law. “The Executive Branch has no constitutional authority to unilaterally impose elections demands on state officials—and certainly no authority to engage in intimidation, threats, and coercion of local election officials for conducting an election in the manner required by federal and state law,” the lawsuit further argues. The next day, a federal judge sided with the unions, temporarily blocking the administration from making intimidating or threatening demands of election officials. “One of the hallmarks of a fair election is the freedom to exercise the right to vote free from threat, fear, or intimidation,” the judge wrote in her ruling. With voting already underway, she warned of the consequences of allowing the threats to continue: “Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.” The Trump administration is appealing the decision. On Nov. 2, 2026, a bipartisan group of 18 former election officials represented by States United filed an amicus brief in the appeal, urging the court to ensure the Trump administration ceases threatening election officials in the midst of an ongoing election in order to have them comply with its demands. Based on their collective experience running elections, the officials explain how the Trump administration’s demands can be intimidating in an already heightened threat environment, seek to upend state and federal law, are infeasible to implement with so little time before an election, and risk disenfranchising voters. Diverting election officials’ time, resources, and energy—during their busiest time of the year—would be extremely disruptive to the administration of the midterms, they argue. “The increased federal pressure and threats on election officials that precipitated this case are part of a pattern by the administration of attempting to assert authority over elections and questioning the integrity of state and local officials,” the group writes. “In our collective experience as election officials, we have never seen such a concerted fixation by the federal government on election workers through letters, subpoenas, press conferences, and social media posts, threatening them with imprisonment if they do not accede to certain demands.” This is a joint website of the States United Democracy Center and States United Action. title: Congressional Oversight after Trump v. United States - Lawfare
content: The upcoming main navigation can be gotten through utilizing the tab key. Any buttons that open a sub navigation can be triggered by the space or enter key. The Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States has been widely recognized as a “dramatic, radical expansion” of presidential power. But one implication of that expansion, which has thus far received little attention, is how in bolstering the “conclusive and preclusive” nature of core executive powers, the decision shrunk the “legislative” space where Congress can conduct oversight. In other words, Trump v. United States diminished not only Congress’s power to legislate with respect to the executive branch but also Congress’s power to investigate it. The full ramifications of Trump are not yet known. But, should Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress in the 2026 midterms, the executive branch will almost certainly wield the Trump decision aggressively to resist congressional investigations. Congressional Democrats will undoubtedly reject these broad readings of Trump. But congressional Democrats will also likely make creative arguments to circumvent the decision’s strictures, including potentially by invoking Congress’s power to investigate pursuant to its power to propose constitutional amendments. Congress has investigated the executive branch since the nation’s earliest days, beginning in 1792 when the House of Representatives established a special committee to probe the defeat of U.S. troops under the command of Gen. Arthur St. Clair. But the Constitution does not grant Congress a freestanding investigative power. Rather, the Supreme Court has long understood Congress’s power of inquiry to be auxiliary to Congress’s legislative function. As the Court explained in Trump v. Mazars, when quoting from established precedent, Congress’s oversight power “is justified solely as an adjunct to the legislative process.” Congressional oversight must therefore “concern a subject on which legislation ‘could be had.’” The executive branch has taken the view that this limitation walls off certain core executive branch functions—such as the president’s pardon and removal powers—from congressional oversight. The executive branch invoked this argument when resisting congressional inquiries into President Clinton’s grant of clemency to Puerto Rican militants and President George W. Bush’s dismissal and replacement of U.S. attorneys. The executive branch, however, still coupled its arguments about the illegitimacy of the probes with formal assertions of executive privilege. Under this belt-and-suspenders approach, the executive branch essentially argued that Congress’s request was likely illegitimate because it strayed outside Congress’s legislative authority, but that even assuming Congress had oversight authority, the information was protected by executive privilege because the executive branch’s confidentiality interests outweighed any congressional need. The Supreme Court’s 2024 Trump decision powerfully bolsters the executive branch’s contention that certain core executive functions are off limits from congressional oversight. Much of the attention has understandably focused on the results of that case—an effectively fatal blow to Special Counsel Jack Smith’s efforts to prosecute President Trump on charges related to election interference. But the decision’s broader reasoning will have important repercussions for future congressional oversight. In assessing the extent to which the president is shielded from federal criminal law, the Supreme Court noted in Trump that “Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President’s actions on subjects within his ‘conclusive and preclusive’ constitutional authority.” In other words, within these domains, the president’s conduct cannot be prosecuted under the law because Congress lacks the power to pass laws that would make the president prosecutable. In an echo of the executive branch’s position, the Court listed, among other things, the president’s pardon and removal powers as areas within the president’s exclusive constitutional authority. The Court also stated that “the Executive Branch has ‘exclusive authority and absolute discretion’ to decide which crimes to investigate and prosecute” and, relatedly, that the president has “exclusive authority over the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department and its officials.” Again, these statements were made in the context of describing areas of exclusive executive authority in which Congress could not legislate (including to criminalize presidential conduct). The Court did not directly address Congress’s investigative authority. But because it has long been established that Congress “cannot inquire into matters which are within the exclusive province of one of the other branches of the Government,” the executive branch will doubtless invoke Trump to resist congressional oversight. And some of the opinion’s language—such as the executive branch having “exclusive authority over the investigative and prosecutorial functions of the Justice Department”—can be construed quite capaciously. Of course, to Trump’s critics, some of his actions in these “exclusive” domains are among the most troubling of his second term in office. His detractors have, for example, criticized the alleged targeting of Trump’s political foes for criminal prosecution, as well as his pardons. Democrats have made clear that, should they retake control of one or both chambers of Congress, investigations into both areas will be among their highest oversight priorities. The executive branch will almost certainly rely on Trump as a powerful tool to oppose Congress’s demands. Congress will push back. As an initial matter, Congress is likely to contest an expansive reading of Trump that puts broad swaths of executive branch activity outside the reach of Congress’s legislative oversight. Congress may also get creative in its investigative rationales, attempting to justify informational requests touching on the exercise of core executive authority by saying such information is needed to inform legislation that sits outside such core executive areas. For instance, expect Congress to contend that it requires information about presidential clemency decisions not because Congress is seeking to regulate the president’s own exercise of the pardon power but because it is attempting to regulate the conduct of pardon applicants or recipients. And Congress may invoke other authorities in support of its investigations. While Trump cabined Congress’s authority to legislate (and so investigate pursuant to that legislative authority), Congress has other authorities beyond its legislative power. Congress may well explore using these other authorities to investigate exercises of core executive powers. For example, Congress could investigate using its impeachment powers. Jonathan Shaub proposes this path in one of the few treatments to date of the oversight implications of Trump (another text that addresses these implications is the most recent edition of When Congress Comes Calling, a congressional oversight handbook that Jenner & Block and the Project on Government Oversight updated in 2025). The power to impeach encompasses a corresponding power to investigate. And, because impeachments target “treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors,” investigations conducted pursuant to the impeachment power are widely understood to have greater reach than investigations conducted as part of ordinary legislative oversight. President Polk once said that the House, in exercising its impeachment power, could “penetrate into the most secret recesses of the executive departments.” At the same time, the impeachment power has significant limitations. It resides solely with the House—the Senate cannot invoke it. And it reflects a grave step that can be both politically costly and polarizing. In today’s climate, any investigation that proceeds under the banner of impeachment would likely lose any hope of broad bipartisan support, even on subjects where there might otherwise be shared interest in reform. As an alternative, Congress may well justify contested investigations by asserting that the investigations are an exercise of Congress’s power to propose constitutional amendments. Article V of the Constitution provides that “Congress, whenever two thirds of both houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose amendments to this Constitution.” Congress may argue that the same logic that permits Congress to investigate pursuant to its legislative function—namely, that “without information, Congress would be shooting in the dark, unable to legislate ‘wisely or effectively’”—likewise supports Congress’s ability to investigate pursuant to this amendment power. Without the ability to inform itself, how would Congress be able to “deem it necessary” to propose an amendment? And, Congress would likely say, because a constitutional amendment can alter the Constitution’s existing delegation of powers across the branches, Congress should be able to inquire into areas of authority that, at present, are allocated exclusively to the other branches. Congress might well argue, for example, that in considering whether to propose an amendment to the president’s pardon power, it is important to understand how presidents have actually exercised it. This would not be the first time that Congress conducted fact finding as it considered constitutional amendments. The Senate Committee on the Judiciary, for instance, has held hearings to consider constitutional amendments that would permit more stringent campaign finance laws. (Among the witnesses at a 2014 hearing on the subject was then-Professor Jamie Raskin, now the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, the House Committee responsible for constitutional amendments.) As another, earlier, example, Congress held hearings on the Equal Rights Amendment before sending it to the states for ratification. And in the wake of the Civil War, the Joint Committee on Reconstruction “conducted hearings and grappled with the constitutional questions that followed emancipation.” The Joint Committee, “authorized to send for persons and papers,” heard testimony from 144 witnesses and introduced, among other things, what ultimately became the 14th Amendment. So there is arguably precedent that Congress could invoke for a distinct power of inquiry pursuant to Article V. The executive branch would likely object, of course. One potential objection is that this “constitutional oversight” power could be used simply as an end run around the current restrictions on Congress’s legislative oversight. That there are certain areas, entrusted to the other branches, that Congress cannot investigate pursuant to its legislative powers reflects the separation of powers enshrined in the Constitution. Congress, the argument would go, should not be able to circumvent the Constitution’s existing structure—and thereby invade the separation of powers—by invoking the mere possibility of changing that structure. In turn, Congress might reply that, because an amendment can, by definition, alter the scope of Article II, the executive cannot use Article II as a shield to block Congress’s inquiry into whether it should be amended. Additionally, even on subjects where Congress may unquestionably request information from the executive branch, the executive branch may still claim that its confidentiality interests in the requested information outweigh Congress’s need for that information. So the branches would likely also argue over the standard an Article V informational demand must meet to overcome such confidentiality claims. It is commonly understood, for instance, that Congress’s informational needs are considered less weighty in the context of legislation than impeachment, not least because, to borrow from an influential en banc opinion from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, “legislative judgments normally depend more on the predicted consequences of proposed legislative actions and their political acceptability, than on precise reconstruction of past events.” Perhaps, under this same logic, Article V informational demands would be accorded equal or even lesser weight than legislative demands—the latter of which might mitigate concerns that such demands are purely an end run around the limits on Congress’s legislative oversight authority. One could imagine a sliding scale where investigative demands pursuant to the impeachment power would be the narrowest in scope but the most penetrating in reach; demands pursuant to the amendment power would be broadest in scope but least powerful in the face of executive objections; and demands pursuant to legislative oversight would be somewhere in the middle. Among its many ramifications, Trump has quietly weakened Congress’s ability to conduct legislative oversight over the executive branch. As a result, a Congress hostile to the executive branch will likely look for alternative paths to pursue its investigative priorities. Congress’s authority to investigate pursuant to its Article V power to propose amendments has been undertheorized, perhaps because, under a more capacious understanding of Congress’s authority to conduct legislative oversight, there has been little need to explore alternatives. But now, if Democrats control one or both houses in the next Congress, the coming years may see Congress invoke its Article V authority in order to investigate areas of the executive branch that might otherwise be off limits.

title: ‘Billie’ Is a 650-HP Modified Pontiac GTO from Ringbrothers - Car and Driver
content: Ringbrothers is back at SEMA with a customized 1965 Pontiac, featuring carbon-fiber bodywork and an LT4 supercharged V-8 engine. The 2026 SEMA show opened today, celebrating the unbridled imagination of the custom car scene, and, of course, Wisconsin-based Ringbrothers has returned with yet another exquisite creation. This year’s showpiece is a 1965 Pontiac GTO convertible dubbed “Billie,” which enhances the classic muscle car’s assertive styling and packs it with modern power. Ringbrothers built Billie for a customer who wanted to pay tribute to a GTO his mother once owned. The client originally proposed the name “Goat,” with Ringbrothers suggesting Billie (as in billy goat), a more playful take on the iconic Pontiac’s long-held nickname. Despite presenting as a GTO, Billie originally started life as a 1965 Pontiac Tempest, before Ringbrothers went to work, widening the body by five inches, reshaping the front fenders, lengthening the rocker panels, and adding carbon-fiber doors. The hood is also fashioned from carbon fiber and wears billet-aluminum inserts and an enlarged scoop to feed air to the engine. That engine is a Chevy’s LT4 supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, cranking out 650 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque and hooked up to a Bowler Performance 10-speed automatic transmission. The body is placed atop a Roadster Shop Fast Track Stage III chassis, and Billie also features Fox coil-over springs and six-piston Brembo brakes. The staggered HRE G-Code wheels, measuring 19 inches up front and 20 inches at the rear, are shod in Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 rubber. At first glance, Billie looks quite faithful to the original GTO, but look closely, and you’ll notice custom bumpers, new headlight surrounds, and a single-piece machined billet-aluminum taillight panel. Ringbrothers also employed carbon fiber on the lower front end and for the rear bumper section that houses the large exhaust outlets. Adding to the head-turning look is the Billie Goat Blue paint job, a rich, shimmering hue that is contrasted by polished chrome trim. The cabin is outfitted in gray and blue leather, while the dashboard has been pushed four inches forward and two inches lower. Ringbrothers modernized the instrumentation, fitted a new climate-control system, and added an auto-dimming rearview mirror. There’s also a restored factory radio that now has Bluetooth connectivity, and the aluminum trim is paired with a sweet wood shifter. Ringbrothers says the entire build took more than 5500 hours. Billie may not be as radical as some of Ringbrothers’ past projects, such as the LT4-powered Rolls-Royce dubbed “Paramount” or “Enyo,” a 1948 Chevy truck turned into an open-wheel race car, but the modified Pontiac is the perfect representation of the company’s expertise in honing the classic lines of vintage muscle cars. title: The Karma Eximius 1 Swaps 3-Cylinder Range Extender for 6.2-Liter V-8 Power to Make 1200 HP - Road & Track
content: That said, it’s a one-off build, so don’t expect to see similar cars at your local Karma dealer. 14 years after the debut of the original Fisker Karma, successor brand Karma Automotive is still trying to build a future beyond that car. It has grand plans to do so with a new two-door GT and an SUV—but in the meantime, the basic Fisker Karma platform is still evolving. The latest Karma model takes the basic shape of the original car to its wildest extreme yet: a one-off called the Eximius 1. The bright blue sedan retains the basic shape of the Gyesera four-door first unveiled in 2024, but its three-cylinder series hybrid powertrain has been replaced by something substantially more powerful. Karma says that the Eximius 1 features a 6.2-liter V-8 pushing out 550 horsepower, which is paired with 645 hp from its batteries for a peak system output of 1200 ponies. That gets the car from 0-60 miles per hour in a claimed 2.7 seconds, and the brand says that the one-off is complete with carbon ceramic brakes and a semi-active Ohlens suspension to help keep all that power on the road. While the performance is a huge step up from the Gyesera, the styling changes are even more outrageous. Massive aero elements jut out from the front fenders and rear doors, wrapped in contrasting white to emphasize the widebody look. A front splitter, rear wing, and rear diffuser are all adorned with LED running lights or tail lights, ensuring that the aggressive aerodynamics will be visible at night just as they are in the day. Inside, the Gyesera’s relatively muted cabin is revamped with a mix of bright blue and white materials. Alcantara appears everywhere from the dashboard to the seats, Recaro buckets in both the front and rear of the car. The rear center console is built around an Eximius-branded carbon fiber helmet, secured in position with a bright blue strap that matches the car’s seatbelts. Karma is not saying who exactly ordered the Eximius 1, but the brand does add that the number on the side, 5, is “of particular significance to the commissioning client.” Given that it is hard to miss, the owner should be fairly easy to spot the first time they take it out for a drive in public. Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. title: Albertsons v. Kroger trial wraps in Delaware, case remains far from over - Boise State Public Radio
content: Boise-based Albertsons is seeking more than $8 billion in damages and interest from Kroger after the grocery giants’ proposed $25 billion merger fell apart in 2024. The two companies recently presented their arguments during a trial in Delaware’s Court of Chancery. Jennifer Kay, a senior correspondent for Bloomberg Law, covered the proceedings and joined Boise State Public Radio’s Morning Edition to discuss the case and what comes next. The following transcript was generated by software and edited by a human. Troy Oppie, BSPR: It's Morning Edition on Boise State Public Radio News. Good morning, I'm Troy Oppie. After their nearly $25 billion merger deal fell apart, Boise-based Albertsons sued fellow grocery giant Kroger, blaming Kroger for the deal getting blocked by regulators. Albertsons wants more than $8 billion from Kroger in damages and interest. Kroger has accused Albertsons of working behind the scenes to undermine the deal, leading to its failure. The two sides were in court the last two weeks in October, laying out their case before a Delaware Court of Chancery judge. And we're joined this morning by Jennifer Kay, Senior Correspondent for Bloomberg Law, who covered the trial. Good morning, Jennifer. Thanks for being here. Oppie: Let's first start with what is the Court of Chancery? Kay: The Court of Chancery. If you know about it at all, it's because it's the premier M&A dispute venue in the country. Most of the fortune 500 is registered for business here in the state of Delaware. So anytime there's a lawsuit or litigation involving those companies, either between the companies themselves, as in this case, or involving their shareholders. It goes to court in a special business court here in Delaware called the Chancery Court. Oppie: So in this trial, Albertsons wants billions of dollars in penalties because it says Kroger did not do enough of the right kind of due diligence to satisfy regulators. How did they lay out that argument in court, and who are the witnesses they relied upon to do that? Kay: So you had the former CEOs of both Albertsons and Kroger testifying. These were the leaders, Vivek Sankaran and Rodney McMullen. They were the two leaders who were kind of guiding the companies through the merger process, and then that merger ultimately failed. They both took the stand and had wildly divergent views of what happened. You also have the current Albertsons CEO testifying during trial. She had been looking to kind of elevate her role at Albertsons at the time through the merger. It didn't quite work out the way she thought it would, but she's ended up as CEO of Albertsons now. And then you also have had all of the antitrust attorneys and the deal counsel, the lawyers who basically helped guide the companies through the merger process, through the regulatory review. They've been on the stand talking about what kind of things they were thinking about as they advised the company. Oppie: You know, sometimes in court cases, folks watching can get a read on a judge, you know, based on the questions that they're asking, where they might be leaning. Did you get any any sense of how the judge might be interpreting this case during that testimony? Kay: In Chancery court, it's just the judge. No jury. She's going to make an opinion by herself. And she hasn't asked too many questions throughout trial. And it's been a full ten days of 9-to-5 testimony. But her questions that she has asked have focused really on the technicalities of the divestitures. That was the process where Kroger and Albertsons were proposing to sell off hundreds of stores in order to meet regulatory approval. What the judge, Vice Chancellor Lori Will, has been asking. She's been focused on the methodology for how those stores were selected, how they landed on a certain number of stores in various proposals. She's really kind of gotten into the like economic ratios that were at play. Oppie: Kroger, for its part, in pretrial filings has accused Albertsons of working to undermine the deal, specifically keying in on then chief operating officer and now CEO of Albertsons, Susan Morris. How did that play out in court? Kay: The former Kroger CEO, Rodney McMullen, testified that there was a, quote unquote, suspicion that Albertsons was having conversations behind Kroger's back about the divestitures, about the third party that was supposed to be buying those stores, and what Susan Morris's role might have been. Morris, when she took the stand, she said, look, Rodney McMullen had come to her with some vague statements about her having a role in the combined entity once the merger closed, but there were never any specifics about that. So then she was approached by CNS, the company that was supposed to be buying the hundreds of stores that were going to be sold off through the merger. And she liked the idea of that. And CNS came to her with a really solid plan for what she was going to be doing. She was going to be leading the stores that were going to be sold off and really make CNS, which is focused on wholesaling. She was going to be building up its retail presence, and she said, 'yeah, I was talking to them with my personal email through my personal channels, but that's because I didn't think it was proper for me to negotiate an employment contract with them while using my Albertsons contacts.' And she testified that, 'no, I didn't give confidential information about the merger or about Kroger or about Albertson's to this other company.' Oppie: So what's next for this trial? This is another unique thing about Court of Chancery is that this is not even close to the end of this trial. Kay: This is a case that's been hanging around since 2024, and it is not going to be over until maybe the midpoint of next year. That's because a trial is really just an opportunity for the judge to hear witness testimony. And then in a couple of months, probably sometime in February, just the attorneys will come back and argue before the judge as to why their witnesses did or did not provide evidence that supports their arguments. And then about three months after that, sometimes longer, that's when the judge will issue her opinion. Oppie: And if either side doesn't like that opinion, they can appeal to the Delaware State Supreme Court. Kay: Right, they go right to the state Supreme Court. And so that adds another six months to a year to the process. Oppie: Jennifer Kay is senior correspondent with Bloomberg Law, covering the Albertsons and Kroger trial over the two companies failed merger. Thanks so much for spending some time with us in Boise this morning. title: Decoded - Technology Law Insights, V 7, Issue 10, 2026 - JD Supra
content:
Welcome to our tenth issue of 2026 of Decoded -- our technology law insights e-newsletter. This is our second-to-last issue of the year. We truly appreciate your readership. As we are planning our last issue of 2026 and look forward to 2027. Nicholas P. Mooney II, Co-Editor of Decoded; Chair of Spilman's Technology Practice Group; Co-Chair of the Cybersecurity & Data Protection Practice Group; and Co-Chair of the Artificial Intelligence Law Practice Group Alexander L. Turner, Co-Editor of Decoded and Co-Chair of the Cybersecurity & Data Protection Practice Group AI Adoption by Industry Shows What Other Sectors can Learn “Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy.” Why this is important: Silicon Valley is leading in adopting new technology. If that were the end of this summary, you would justifiably leave unimpressed. The more useful point is what comes next: these tools permeate other sectors on a lag, and those not yet on the cutting edge can follow the blueprint the trailblazers are drawing right now. The TripleTen-sponsored survey behind the piece breaks adoption down by industry, and after tech, finance is the clear runner-up: 48 percent of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots and 47 percent say AI has changed the job "a lot." Healthcare and education sit at the other end, with 18 percent and 25 percent asked to use chatbots and 41 percent of healthcare workers reporting AI hasn't changed their job at all. These sectors run on a mix of hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional staff, and back-office teams, which makes uniform adoption a slow proposition by design. Compliance pressures and human-facing work only reinforce the deliberate pace. Yet no one is standing still: 79 percent of workers were asked to learn at least one skill they didn't previously have. So the lesson for a slower-moving field isn't to panic; it's to use the lag. Watch which skills actually produce results in tech and finance, build those now, and you'll meet the shift prepared instead of surprised. --- Christopher M. Green Businesses Need More Integrated Risk Management to Counter Cyberattacks, AI-Powered Fraud “Risks are growing at a time when companies rely more than ever on vendors for cybersecurity, according to a new report.” Why this is important: A new survey of 1,100 business leaders by the advisory firm Grant Thornton found a striking gap between worry and readiness. About three-quarters of leaders said a cyberattack is one of the biggest threats to their business over the next two years, yet only about half were confident they could spot a sophisticated attack while it was happening. The survey also found that nearly every organization, 96 percent, now relies on outside companies to help detect and respond to cyber threats. That is often a smart choice, since skilled security staff is hard to hire. But only about one in four leaders said those outside providers are truly connected to their own internal processes. Meanwhile, more than half of leaders named fraud powered by artificial intelligence (AI), such as convincing fake emails, voices, and videos, as a major concern. What this means for your business: Risk tends to fall through the cracks when different teams each see only their own piece of the picture. Grant Thornton recommends bringing cybersecurity, compliance, and audit functions together around a shared view of risk, with clear ownership and common definitions. In practical terms, that means making sure your security vendors and your internal team are working from the same information and know who does what when something goes wrong. Outsourcing security can strengthen a business, but it does not outsource responsibility. The best time to confirm everyone knows their role is before an incident, not during one. --- James E. Dunlap, Chief Information Officer, Spilman Thomas & Battle $80 Million Settlement Proposed to Resolve Conduent Data Breach Litigation “It was the largest healthcare data breach reported in 2025 and ranks as the third-largest healthcare data breach of all time.” Why this is important: Business-services giant Conduent has proposed an $80 million settlement to resolve consolidated class litigation in the District of New Jersey over a 2024–2025 cyberattack that compromised the data of roughly 62.2 million people. The SafePay ransomware group claimed to have exfiltrated 8.5 terabytes of data, including names, addresses, dates of birth, medical and health-insurance information, and Social Security numbers. By volume, it ranks as the largest healthcare data breach reported in 2025 and the third-largest of all time. The settlement divides the class into two subclasses and offers a year of credit or medical-data monitoring, reimbursement of up to $3,500 in documented losses, and pro rata cash payments, with California residents eligible for an extra 20 percent. The lawsuit reflects two features of today’s cyber-risk landscape: ransomware crews like SafePay increasingly steal and threaten to publish data rather than merely encrypting it, and the real exposure often sits with back-office vendors and processors — Conduent handles data for government agencies, health plans, and employers — whose breaches cascade across millions of individuals who never chose to do business with them. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II Healthcare’s Agentic AI Boom is Outpacing Governance: Report “Patient safety could be at risk if agentic AI tools are rolled out without proper guardrails, Imprivata’s chief medical and growth officer warns.” Why this is important: Healthcare organizations are rapidly adopting agentic AI, but governance and oversight practices are struggling to keep pace. A survey found that more than one-quarter of healthcare organizations have implemented agentic AI, while another 44 percent are piloting or conducting proof-of-concept projects. Although more than 85 percent of AI leaders express confidence in their ability to monitor and control autonomous agents, 72 percent acknowledge that AI tools are deployed without IT approval at least occasionally. The governance gap presents significant legal, security, and patient-safety risks. Unlike conventional software, autonomous agents can independently access systems and execute actions, potentially exposing patient information, altering medical records or medications, or acting beyond a clinician’s intent. Risks increase as agents receive broader permissions and operate across multiple systems. The survey highlights fragmented governance approaches and uncertainty regarding appropriate human oversight. For healthcare organizations, effective governance should include defined agent identities, permissions and operational boundaries, risk-based human review, and auditable activity trails, particularly for higher-risk clinical applications. --- Shane P. Riley Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents to Breach Company Websites, Target Over 1,200 Sites “A Chinese-speaking criminal pointed autonomous AI agents at company websites and let them break in with almost no help, and a security researcher watched it happen because the operators left their control panels open on the internet.” Why this is important: Imagine a burglar who no longer must case each house himself but can send out a team of robots to test every door and window in the neighborhood. That is essentially what happened here. A criminal used artificial intelligence (AI) “agents,” programs that can pursue a goal on their own, to break into company websites with very little human direction. The agents probed more than 1,200 websites and reached sites belonging to more than 100 companies, including well-known names like Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. A security researcher uncovered the campaign only because the attackers carelessly left their control panels open on the internet. The cost to the criminal was remarkably low: about $5,000 for the entire campaign, or roughly $50 per successful break-in. What this means for your business: Hacking is becoming cheaper, faster, and easier. Attacks that once took weeks for a skilled criminal can now be launched by one person with an AI tool and a modest budget, which means no business is too small to be a target. The encouraging news is that these AI agents succeeded by exploiting ordinary weaknesses, such as outdated website software. Keeping your website and the systems behind it up to date and confirming that any vendor managing your website does the same remains one of the most effective defenses available. --- James E. Dunlap, Chief Information Officer, Spilman Thomas & Battle Health Information Privacy Reform Act Advanced by HELP Committee “If passed, within 18 months of enactment, the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the Federal Trade Commission, is required to promulgate regulations establishing and implementing HIPAA-like privacy, security, and breach notification standards for ‘applicable health information’ processed by regulated entities and their service providers.” Why this is important: The Health Information Privacy Reform Act seeks to close gaps in federal privacy protections for health information collected outside the HIPAA framework. The amended bill was advanced unanimously by the HELP Committee and would extend HIPAA-like privacy, security, and breach-notification requirements to “consumer health data” collected by non-HIPAA-regulated entities, including health apps, wearable devices, and other consumer technologies. If enacted, HHS, in consultation with the FTC, would have 18 months to establish implementing regulations addressing permitted and prohibited uses and disclosures, individual authorization, data minimization, and minimum-necessary requirements. Individuals would receive rights comparable to HIPAA rights, including access, amendment, portability, and deletion within 30 days. Covered entities would also face HIPAA-like administrative, technical, and physical safeguards and breach-notification obligations. The legislation also has significant implications for emerging health data uses. HHS would be required to issue guidance concerning HIPAA-protected data used with artificial intelligence and machine learning systems and the application of the minimum necessary standard. The bill would establish national de-identification standards and permit states to impose stronger privacy requirements, potentially preserving a complex state-law compliance landscape. For healthcare, technology, and life-sciences companies, the proposal could materially expand compliance obligations for consumer-generated health data and create new risks concerning data collection, disclosure, cybersecurity, AI development, and data monetization. --- Shane P. Riley US Companies Set to Pay $1.4 Billion in Privacy Settlements Over Web and App Tracking, up 36% From 2025 “Privado AI's 2026 Website & App Privacy Litigation Report analyzed 116 US class action settlements and found the average payout now stands at $6.7 million, with lawsuits up 18-fold since 2022, from around 200 filings to a projected 3,500 this year.” Why this is important: A new report from Privado AI projects that U.S. companies will pay more than $1.4 billion in 2026 to settle claims that their websites and apps shared users’ personal data without proper consent — a 36 percent jump over 2025, with the average settlement now $6.7 million. The litigation wave is striking in scale: annual filings have climbed roughly eighteenfold, from about 200 in 2022 to a projected 3,500 this year. Much of the surge is powered by creative use of old statutes — the federal Wiretap Act of 1968 appears in 53 percent of 2026 settlements and the California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA), passed in 1967 to curb covert recording of phone calls, in 43 percent, because these wiretapping laws allow private suits with fixed per-violation damages, whereas newer privacy statutes like the CCPA are enforceable only by regulators. Plaintiffs typically argue that third-party tracking pixels and cookies “intercept” a visitor’s communications in real time, and Meta’s advertising pixel alone is named in 91 percent of settlements that identify a third-party tracker. Healthcare companies account for 64 percent of settlements — a reflection of how sensitive site data is and of federal scrutiny of tracking tools on patient portals — while technology companies pay the most on average, driven by two large Google settlements. The article’s and report’s numbers are striking, but the real numbers aren’t even known. The settlements that make up the report are only those that are public. The report estimates that as many as 100,000 private settlements took place between 2022 and 2025; those settlements aren’t reflected in the report’s numbers. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II Former OpenAI Researcher Issues Grim Warning, Says Only 5,000 People have Access to Frontier AI While 2 Billion Use It as ‘Better Google Search’ “Former OpenAI researcher Andrej Karpathy warned that the gap between public understanding of artificial intelligence and its most advanced capabilities is widening, with a small group of professionals witnessing a rapid leap in what AI agents can accomplish.” Why this is important: Mind the [widening] gap. London rail passengers are intimately familiar with this warning. It appears that AI resisters should be as well. Andrej Karpathy, a former OpenAI researcher, posted on X (formerly Twitter) that the gap between the AI "haves" and the AI "have nots" is "widening," becoming a sharper funnel. He estimated that the wide end of the funnel includes around 6 billion people (75 percent) who have barely interacted with LLMs, and around 1-2 billion people (20 percent) who use free-tier products like a better Google search. In contrast, the narrow end of the funnel includes around 20 million people (0.2 percent) who use frontier-grade LLMs and "see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt," and 5,000 people (0.00006 percent) use frontier-grade systems and coordinate swarms of agents in collaboration over weeks to do things that would have taken top industry professionals years of work. The uncomfortable thing about the gap is that it's partially self-inflicted at the wide end. Many are standing on the platform insisting the train isn't moving, their verdict formed on a free-tier chatbot already out of date. How this shakes out is the real question: either seeing will become believing as access widens, or the gap becomes a genuine divide between those who adopted and those who resisted. It closes one informed user at a time, so before you decide where you land, go use the frontier tools on something you know well and see the results for yourself. --- Christopher M. Green Amazon and Ring Seek Dismissal of Familiar Faces Biometric Privacy Lawsuit “Defense says plaintiffs have not shown their own faces were processed and cannot use broader state laws to create biometric claims lawmakers did not authorize.” Why this is important: Amazon and its Ring subsidiary have asked a federal judge to dismiss a proposed class action challenging Ring’s “Familiar Faces” feature, which lets participating doorbell cameras recognize recurring visitors and tell the owner who is at the door. What makes the lawsuit unusual is that the named plaintiffs are not Ring customers but bystanders — people whose faces may be scanned as they walk past or visit a property, allegedly without their knowledge or consent. Amazon’s motion to dismiss presses two arguments: that the plaintiffs have not plausibly alleged their own faces were ever processed, and that plaintiffs are improperly stretching consumer-protection and common-law theories to manufacture biometric claims that lawmakers haven’t expressly authorized. The case is important because it tests whether biometric privacy can be litigated outside of places like Illinois, which has enacted its Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), a law which expressly regulates the collection and storage of biometric information. A ruling for the plaintiffs in the Ring case could open consumer-protection statutes nationwide as a vehicle for biometric claims; a ruling for Amazon would reinforce that, absent a BIPA-style law, bystanders have little recourse. --- Nicholas P. Mooney II How Construction is Dealing with Cybersecurity in the Age of AI “Namely, the major contractors building government projects across the U.S. house not only personal information within their tech stacks, but also what amounts to state secrets.” Why this is important: With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence, every facet of operating a complex construction business has become more challenging, not least of which is cybersecurity. Construction firms are not immune to the risks posed by cybersecurity breaches, especially those fueled by AI, and the general attitude of the industry has not been overly responsive to the risk of potential breaches. Some industry leaders and legal experts have been proactive in warning the rest of the industry of the dangers posed by cybersecurity breaches and the steps that must be taken to mitigate the risks. After all, it is not a matter of if a breach occurs, but when. The most important step is to take the risk seriously. Many firms in the industry do not see the risk as substantial and even assume that they aren’t large enough to attract the attention of a malicious actor. Experts disagree. The size of a firm is not a shield from the dangers of an attack, and with the advancement of AI agents, smaller firms are more attractive targets due to their relative lack of protections and their access to sensitive information. In response to the assumption that small firms fly under the radar of malicious actors, Richard Volack, a partner at New York City-based Peckar & Abramson, is quoted as saying “[y]ou may think you have nothing that the hackers want, but you have a whole bunch.” Firms of all sizes must take steps to protect themselves from malicious actors who will inevitably target them for cyberattacks. Constant testing of internal security systems, regular employee training and awareness, and liability insurance in the event of a breach are just some of the steps that firms should take to protect themselves and their customers from cybersecurity threats. The cost of preventative measures, though steep, pales in comparison to the cost of a breach. In the case of breach-related wire fraud, Volack emphasized that “[i]f you’re past say 24 or 48 hours [of the wire], then it’s harder, if not impossible to put a hold on the bank,” potentially resulting in massive monetary losses. In some cases, breaches can even lead to claims under the False Claims Act if contractors’ cybersecurity efforts are determined to be inadequate after the fact. Cybersecurity risks are an ever-expanding danger to firms in the construction industry, and effectively combatting those risks requires preemptive action. As the saying goes, the best defense is a good offense, and when it comes to cybersecurity, aggressively pursuing preventative measures is that offense. --- Jonathan E.
