title: Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos - SCOTUSblog
content: In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work. But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.” Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends. Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all. Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs. Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point. In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read: “[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.” “But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.” “Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.” After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all. In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading. But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs. In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting. Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.” Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.” In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank: In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs. For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front. In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice. Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point. Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed. title: Predicted Newcastle United team v Everton with five changes tonight - Yahoo Sports
content: Matthias Jaissle and his players looking to build on last weekend's Premier League victory at Selhurst Park. Whilst at the same time bounce back from the Carabao Cup defeat at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday. Everton going through to the quarter-finals and a trip to League Two Fleetwood Town. Tonight though a chance for Newcastle United to get back on track and for the Premier League table to look far better by the close of play on Monday. A win against Everton would take Matthias Jaissle's side up to seventh in the table with 14 points, the same number as Brentford in sixth and only a point behind Liverpool in fifth. As a reminder, this was the Newcastle United team v Everton on Thursday night: Hornicek, Dedic, Schar, Burn, Hall, Gonzalez, Willock, Ramsey, Barnes, Murphy, Osula Ewen Jaouen and Tino Livramento remain unavailable. Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Lewis Miley have missed recent matches, so it remains to be seen if they will be available. William Osula is also a doubt, forced off on Thursday with a twisted ankle, the NUFC Head Coach saying it was an unknown whether the striker would be okay for this Monday night rematch. This is my predicted Newcastle United team v Everton: Hornicek, Dedic, Thiaw, Burn, Hall, Gonzalez, Willock, Joelinton, Fernandez-Pardo, Elanga, Wissa If I am proved correct it would mean five changes from Thursday night. I don't think Fabian Schar has done anything wrong but I always felt it was a temporary thing to give Malick Thiaw a break and I fancy we will see him alongside Dan Burn given a chance to try and get United more solid at the back. I assume the medical staff wouldn't have wanted Joelinton starting Sunday-Thursday-Monday after having only recently returned to the matchday squad. So after starting on the bench away at Everton, I think the Brazil international will return to the starting line-up tonight. Obviously much depends on who is available tonight but I am predicting a completely different front three. Anthony Elanga will hopefully now be able to start after his sub appearances and a no-brainer for him to replace Jacob Murphy. I'm sure Matthias Jaissle would love to see United pressure Everton from the first whistle to try and get at them. If available I think Matias Fernandez-Pardo will replace Barnes and join Elanga in the team tonight to help do a high press. In my opinion William Osula would probably start again if available but seeing how he limped off on Thursday that looks unlikely to me. Playing MFP through the middle hasn't been a success so far and therefore I see the Belgian on the left and Yoane Wissa returning to play through the middle if Osula is unavailable.

                             (2026) Cite this article There is an unmet need for repigmentation therapies for patients with nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV) who are candidates for systemic therapy. Here, 52-week primary results are reported from two parallel phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of once-daily povorcitinib (oral, highly selective JAK1 inhibitor) 30 mg in adults with moderate-to-severe NSV (STOP-V1 and STOP-V2). STOP-V1 and STOP-V2 enrolled 467 and 449 patients, respectively. In both studies, the primary endpoint of ≥75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) at week 52 was met, demonstrating statistically significant and clinically meaningful repigmentation with povorcitinib versus placebo (STOP-V1: 18.9% versus 6.8%; odds ratio, 3.1; 95% confidence interval 1.6–5.9; P = 0.0003; STOP-V2: 18.9% versus 3.1%; odds ratio, 7.5; 95% confidence interval 3.0–18.6; P < 0.0001). Povorcitinib was well tolerated; the percentage of patients with any treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE) was similar between the povorcitinib and placebo groups in both studies (STOP-V1/STOP-V2, 68.7%/66.7% versus 63.7%/62.7%). The most common TEAEs with povorcitinib were nasopharyngitis (STOP-V1/STOP-V2, 11.2%/11.3% versus placebo, 9.8%/11.1%), acne (10.7%/10.8% versus 3.0%/2.2%) and upper respiratory tract infection (6.9%/14.0% versus 9.0%/10.7%). Serious TEAEs were generally single events, and Janus kinase inhibitor class-specific TEAEs were absent or rare. These results support once-daily povorcitinib as an effective and well-tolerated systemic treatment for adults with moderate-to-severe NSV. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT06113445, NCT06113471. Vitiligo is a chronic, autoimmune disease characterized by skin depigmentation resulting from the loss of melanocytes1,2. The global prevalence of diagnosed vitiligo is approximately 0.4%, with rates varying geographically and by age group3,4. Patients with segmental (unilateral distribution) and nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV; bilateral distribution) have distinct clinical characteristics and disease courses; NSV accounts for up to 90% of vitiligo cases5. Segmental vitiligo affects less body surface area (BSA) and responds best to treatment within 2 years of onset, after which other modalities (for example, surgery) may be considered6. Thus, large, controlled trials generally focus on NSV. Vitiligo is associated with other autoimmune conditions, such as thyroid disorders and type 1 diabetes7; psychosocial comorbidities, including depression, anxiety, suicidality and stigmatization8; and an overall reduction in quality of life9,10. Psychosocial and quality-of-life burden are further impacted by increased disease extent and/or visibility of lesions (for example, facial or hand involvement) and are greater in patients with darker skin types9,10,11. The 2026 INTERCEPT study consensus defines vitiligo severity beyond disease extent, including factors of disease activity, lesion visibility and psychosocial burden, among others, as determinants for recommending systemic therapy12. The JAK–STAT signaling pathway has a critical role in the pathophysiology of vitiligo13. Activation of the JAK–STAT pathway leads to the production of CXCL10, which promotes further recruitment of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells responsible for the destruction of melanocytes14,15,16. Ruxolitinib (selective JAK1 and JAK2 inhibitor) cream was the first treatment approved for the repigmentation of NSV17 in several geographic regions, including the USA, Canada, the European Union and the UK. Ruxolitinib cream is indicated in patients aged ≥12 years for twice-daily topical treatment of affected areas up to 10% BSA18,19,20,21. There is a need for effective and well-tolerated therapies for patients with NSV who are candidates for systemic therapy (that is, moderate-to-severe NSV12). Povorcitinib is an oral, highly selective JAK1 inhibitor22 currently being evaluated as a potential treatment for autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including vitiligo. In a phase 2, randomized, dose-ranging study in adults with extensive NSV (≥8% affected BSA), povorcitinib was well tolerated and significantly improved facial and total body repigmentation with 15, 45 and 75 mg once-daily (QD) dosing versus placebo at 6 months, with 27.7%, 36.4% and 29.4% improvement from baseline in facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI) respectively, versus 5.1% for placebo, and 19.1%, 17.8% and 15.7% improvement in total VASI (T-VASI) versus −2.3% for placebo23. Further repigmentation was observed with continued treatment over a period of 1 year. Because no clear dose–response for efficacy was observed in phase 2, the dose for the phase 3 studies was selected based on exposure–response modeling24 to optimize the long-term risk/benefit profile, which is particularly important for use in a chronic autoimmune condition such as vitiligo. Povorcitinib 30 mg QD was predicted to have more favorable efficacy and biomarker profiles versus 15 mg QD, and to have similar efficacy and biomarker profiles with a more favorable safety profile versus 45 and 75 mg QD24. Further, clinical, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data suggested that QD povorcitinib would provide an effective and durable response while avoiding JAK2-mediated pathways that have been associated with cytopenias22,25. Here the 52-week primary results are reported from two identically designed phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials—Selective Treatment of Oral Povorcitinib in Vitiligo (STOP-V1 (NCT06113445) and STOP-V2 (NCT06113471))—evaluating the efficacy and safety of povorcitinib 30 mg QD in adults with moderate-to-severe NSV. In STOP-V1 and STOP-V2, eligible patients aged ≥18 years with NSV, affected facial BSA (F-BSA) ≥0.5% and total BSA (T-BSA) ≥5% (no upper limit) were randomized 1:1 to receive oral povorcitinib 30 mg or placebo QD for a 52-week double-blind, placebo-controlled period followed by a 52-week open-label extension period during which all patients received povorcitinib 30 mg QD (Extended Data Fig. 1). The primary endpoint of the STOP-V studies was the proportion of patients achieving ≥75% improvement from baseline in F-VASI (F-VASI75) at week 52. Key secondary endpoints were the proportion of patients achieving a facial Vitiligo Noticeability Scale (VNS) score of 4 (a lot less noticeable) or 5 (no longer noticeable) at week 52; the proportion of patients achieving ≥50% or ≥75% improvement from baseline in T-VASI (T-VASI50 or T-VASI75) at week 52; and the percentage change from baseline in T-VASI at week 52. Other secondary efficacy endpoints were achievement of ≥50% or ≥90% improvement from baseline in F-VASI (F-VASI50 or F-VASI90), ≥90% improvement from baseline in T-VASI (T-VASI90), Facial Static Investigator Global Assessment (FsIGA) and Static Investigator Global Assessment (sIGA) of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear), and facial and total Patient Global Impression of Change-Vitiligo (F-PaGIC-V and T-PaGIC-V, respectively) of ‘very much improved’ or ‘much improved’ at week 52; the proportion of patients in each category of the FsIGA, sIGA, F-PaGIC-V, T-PaGIC-V and facial color-matching question (patient rating of facial color match between treated vitiligo skin and normal skin) at week 52; and the change from baseline in Vitiligo-Specific Quality of Life (VitiQoL) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at week 52. Safety and tolerability were additional secondary endpoints. The percentage change from baseline in F-VASI was assessed as an exploratory endpoint. The proportion of patients with no increase in T-VASI and the proportion of patients with no new or expanding lesions were assessed in post hoc analyses. A total of 916 adults were enrolled in the STOP-V trials (Fig. 1). In STOP-V1, 467 patients from 81 sites in Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and the USA were randomized to povorcitinib 30 mg (n = 233) or placebo (n = 234) between 29 November 2023 and 26 February 2025; the 52-week placebo-controlled period concluded on 24 February 2026 and the 52-week open-label extension period is ongoing. In STOP-V2, 449 patients from 68 sites in Bulgaria, Canada, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, the UK and the USA were randomized to receive povorcitinib 30 mg (n = 223) or placebo (n = 226) between 27 November 2023 and 18 March 2025; the 52-week placebo-controlled period concluded on 17 March 2026 and the 52-week open-label extension period is ongoing. In STOP-V2, two patients (one in each treatment group) did not receive the study drug and were not included in the safety population. Overall, 82.2% and 82.9% of patients in STOP-V1 and STOP-V2 respectively, completed treatment during the 52-week placebo-controlled period. Discontinuation rates were similar between treatment groups in both studies, with withdrawal by patient being the most common reason for discontinuation (Fig. 1). aScreen failures were permitted to rescreen once at investigator discretion; 14 patients in STOP-V1 and 8 patients in STOP-V2 were randomized after rescreening. bOne patient did not receive ≥1 dose of study drug. cIndicates the primary reason for discontinuation. Patient demographics and baseline clinical characteristics were generally similar across treatment groups and studies (Table 1). Median (range) age was 48.0 (18–89) years in STOP-V1 and 46.0 (18–79) years in STOP-V2. The majority of patients were female (STOP-V1, 55.0%; STOP-V2, 57.0%) and white (STOP-V1, 79.4%; STOP-V2, 84.9%). Patients with all Fitzpatrick skin types were included in both studies; 23.1% and 27.4% of patients in STOP-V1 and STOP-V2 respectively, had skin types IV to VI. Per inclusion criteria, all patients had facial vitiligo. In both studies, >94% of patients had vitiligo present on the trunk, lower extremities, upper extremities and hands; >85% had vitiligo on the head and/or neck (excluding face) and feet. A substantial proportion of patients also had vitiligo on the genitals (STOP-V1, 68.1%; STOP-V2, 72.2%). Patients in STOP-V2 had slightly more widespread disease than those in STOP-V1, as indicated by higher baseline mean F-VASI and T-VASI (1.17 and 23.0 respectively, versus 1.05 and 19.5). Patients in STOP-V2 also had longer disease duration than those in STOP-V1 (median (range), 18.3 (0.1–59.3) years versus 16.2 (0.1–61.9) years); across studies, most patients had vitiligo for >10 years (STOP-V1, 68.5%; STOP-V2, 71.5%) and had stable disease at baseline (STOP-V1, 61.2%; STOP-V2, 70.6%) per investigator assessment of the physical signs of disease activity. Approximately 40% of patients in both studies had received prior medications for vitiligo. Of selected comorbidities, the most common was thyroid disorder, affecting approximately 15% of patients in each study. The primary endpoint of F-VASI75 at week 52 was attained by a significantly greater proportion of patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo in both STOP-V1 (modified nonresponder imputation (mNRI), 18.9% versus 6.8%; odds ratio (OR) 3.1; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.6–5.9; P = 0.0003) and STOP-V2 (mNRI, 18.9% versus 3.1%; OR 7.5; 95% CI 3.0–18.6; P < 0.0001). Observed F-VASI75 response rates continued to increase without plateau to week 52 in both studies (Fig. 2a). a,b, Percentage of patients achieving F-VASI75 (a) and VNS 4 or 5 (b) at each visit are presented as observed, with error bars representing the 95% CI and n indicating the number of patients with available data at each time point. ***P < 0.001 or ****P < 0.0001 for povorcitinib versus placebo at week 52 using the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test with stratification by randomization factors. The overall family-wise type I error was controlled at a two-sided α of 0.05. A gatekeeping approach was applied to adjust for multiplicity. Patients with missing data at week 52 were imputed using mNRI for F-VASI75 (STOP-V1, 18.9% versus 6.8% (n = 233 versus n = 234), P = 0.0003; STOP-V2, 18.9% versus 3.1% (n = 223 versus n = 226), P < 0.0001), and VNS 4 or 5 (STOP-V1, 15.1% versus 3.2% (n = 233 versus n = 234), P < 0.0001; STOP-V2, 10.2% versus 1.6% (n = 223 versus n = 226), P = 0.0002). The key secondary endpoint of facial VNS 4 or 5 at week 52 was self-reported by a significantly higher proportion of patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo in STOP-V1 (mNRI, 15.1% versus 3.2%; OR 5.2; 95% CI 2.2–12.5; P < 0.0001) and STOP-V2 (mNRI, 10.2% versus 1.6%; OR 7.5; 95% CI 2.2–25.6; P = 0.0002). Improved VNS 4 or 5 response rates were observed with povorcitinib versus placebo by the first assessment at week 24 in both studies (Fig. 2b). For total body repigmentation, a higher proportion of patients achieved T-VASI50 at week 52 with povorcitinib versus placebo in STOP-V1 (mNRI, 18.4% versus 6.5%; OR 3.2; 95% CI 1.7–6.2; P = 0.0003) and STOP-V2 (mNRI, 12.9% versus 4.8%; OR 2.9; 95% CI 1.3–6.4; P = 0.0048). In both studies, observed T-VASI50 response rates increased with povorcitinib versus placebo from week 24 onward (Fig. 3a). For T-VASI75 at week 52, response rates were low in both studies. In STOP-V1, T-VASI75 response rates did not differ significantly between povorcitinib and placebo (mNRI, 2.6% versus 1.3%; OR 2.0; 95% CI 0.5–8.2; P = 0.3503); in STOP-V2, a significantly greater proportion of patients achieved T-VASI75 at week 52 with povorcitinib versus placebo (mNRI, 2.3% versus 0%; OR not evaluable owing to the absence of placebo responders; 95% CI not evaluable; P = 0.0393). Observed T-VASI75 response rates increased with povorcitinib versus placebo to week 52 in both studies (Fig. 3b). a,b, Percentage of patients achieving T-VASI50 (a) and T-VASI75 (b). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 or ***P < 0.001 for povorcitinib versus placebo at week 52 using the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test with stratification by randomization factors. The overall family-wise type I error was controlled at a two-sided α of 0.05. A gatekeeping approach was applied to adjust for multiplicity. Patients with missing data at week 52 were imputed using mNRI for T-VASI50 (STOP-V1, 18.4% versus 6.5% (n = 233 versus n = 234), P = 0.0003; STOP-V2, 12.9% versus 4.8% (n = 223 versus n = 226), P = 0.0048) and T-VASI75 (STOP-V1, 2.6% versus 1.3% (n = 233 versus n = 234), P = 0.3503; STOP-V2, 2.3% versus 0% (n = 223 versus n = 226), P = 0.0393). c, Mean change in T-VASI from baseline at each visit as observed. Baseline mean (95% CI) T-VASI for the povorcitinib and placebo groups was 19.5 (17.5–21.5) and 19.5 (17.5–21.4) respectively, in STOP-V1, and 23.1 (20.6–25.5) and 23.0 (20.5–25.6) in STOP-V2. ****P < 0.0001 for the LSM difference between povorcitinib versus placebo at week 52 using an analysis of covariance model with stratification by randomization factors. The overall family-wise type I error was controlled at a two-sided α of 0.05. A gatekeeping approach was applied to adjust for multiplicity. Patients who initiated prohibited therapy with a potential impact on vitiligo outcomes before week 52 were imputed using the baseline T-VASI score. Patients with missing data at week 52 were imputed using multiple imputation (STOP-V1, −24.1% versus −5.7% (n = 233 versus n = 234), P < 0.0001; STOP-V2, −21.1% versus −4.4% (n = 223 versus n = 226), P < 0.0001). Error bars represent the 95% CI and n values are the number of patients with available data at each time point. NS, not significant. Patients had a significantly greater least squares mean (LSM) percentage change from baseline (indicating improvement) in T-VASI at week 52 with povorcitinib versus placebo in STOP-V1 (multiple imputation, −24.1% versus −5.7%; LSM difference, −18.4; 95% CI −24.0 to −12.8; P < 0.0001) and STOP-V2 (multiple imputation, −21.1% versus −4.4%; LSM difference, −16.8; 95% CI −21.9 to −11.7; P < 0.0001). Separation between povorcitinib and placebo groups in the percentage change from baseline in T-VASI was observed by week 12 (second on-treatment visit) in both studies (Fig. 3c). Patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo had greater response rates or improvements in nearly all investigator-assessed (F-VASI50 and F-VASI90 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) and FsIGA and sIGA), and patient-reported secondary outcomes (F-PaGIC-V, T-PaGIC-V, facial color-matching, VitiQoL) at week 52 (Extended Data Table 1). Few patients achieved T-VASI90 at week 52, and changes in HADS anxiety and depression scores were minimal. TEAEs were generally consistent between studies (Table 2). In STOP-V1, 68.7% of patients in the povorcitinib group and 63.7% in the placebo group experienced any TEAE during the 52-week placebo-controlled period. In STOP-V2, 66.7% and 62.7% of patients respectively, experienced any TEAE. The most common TEAEs with povorcitinib (occurring in ≥5% of patients in either study) were nasopharyngitis (STOP-V1, 11.2%; STOP-V2, 11.3%), acne (STOP-V1, 10.7%; STOP-V2, 10.8%), upper respiratory tract infection (STOP-V1, 6.9%; STOP-V2, 14.0%), blood creatine phosphokinase (CPK) increase (STOP-V1, 6.9%; STOP-V2, 6.3%), headache (STOP-V1, 5.2%; STOP-V2, 6.8%), influenza (STOP-V1, 3.9%; STOP-V2, 5.0%), sinusitis (STOP-V1, 2.6%; STOP-V2, 5.0%) and hypercholesterolemia (STOP-V1, 0.9%; STOP-V2, 5.0%). Although CPK elevations were among the most common TEAEs, overall blood levels were similar to baseline in most patients (Extended Data Fig. 3). Treatment-related TEAEs occurred in 30.9% of patients in the povorcitinib group and in 21.4% of patients in the placebo group in STOP-V1, and in 33.3% and 18.7% of patients respectively, in STOP-V2. The most common TEAEs considered by investigators as related to povorcitinib treatment (occurring in >3% of patients in either study) were acne (STOP-V1, 10.3%; STOP-V2, 10.4%), headache (STOP-V1, 3.0%; STOP-V2, 4.1%), upper respiratory tract infection (STOP-V1, 1.7%; STOP-V2, 4.5%), blood CPK increase (STOP-V1, 2.1%; STOP-V2, 3.2%) and hypercholesterolemia (STOP-V1, 0.9%; STOP-V2, 4.1%). Increased blood CPK was the most common grade ≥3 TEAE; none were considered serious. Most were asymptomatic and attributed to intense exercise or physical activity. The frequency of serious TEAEs was similar between treatment groups in both studies. Nearly all serious TEAEs were single events (Extended Data Table 2), with only one occurring in >1 patient in either study (urinary tract infection (n = 2) in the povorcitinib group in STOP-V1). Discontinuations owing to TEAEs were slightly higher with povorcitinib versus placebo in both studies. Only one TEAE led to discontinuation of povorcitinib in >1 patient in either study (blood CPK increased; n = 4 in STOP-V1 and n = 1 in STOP-V2; demographics consistent with the overall population); four of these events were attributed to intense physical training or work-related physical exertion and one was of unknown cause. Discontinuations due to increased CPK events were based on prespecified protocol stopping criteria (CPK >5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN) 3 weeks after the first elevated CPK event) rather than clinical symptoms. The frequency of JAK inhibitor class-specific TEAEs (protocol-defined TEAEs of special interest) was generally similar between povorcitinib and placebo in both studies (STOP-V1, 3.0% versus 2.1%; STOP-V2, 2.3% versus 2.2%), and these events were rare (Table 2). There were no occurrences of major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE), tuberculosis or mortality. Nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) or keratinocyte carcinoma occurred in four patients who received povorcitinib (basal cell carcinoma: STOP-V1, n = 1; STOP-V2, n = 3) and none who received placebo; all were grade 1 or 2 in severity and resolved during the study. Only one of these events (grade 2 left frontal basal cell carcinoma) was considered related to treatment and led to discontinuation; this patient (Fitzpatrick skin type II) had prior treatment with UVB phototherapy for 4 years and a topical calcineurin inhibitor for 7 years. One other patient with basal cell carcinoma during the study had previously received phototherapy and had a history of squamous cell carcinoma in situ and basal cell carcinoma (adequately treated and excised) before study enrollment. No other types of malignancy occurred in patients in the povorcitinib group in either study. One patient who received povorcitinib in STOP-V2 experienced pulmonary embolism (grade 3; serious; resolved), thrombosed varicose vein (grade 3; nonserious; resolved) and deep vein thrombosis (grade 3; nonserious; resolving); these events were considered related to povorcitinib treatment and povorcitinib was discontinued. The investigator considered an event of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection (which persisted for >4 months and resolved 5 weeks before the pulmonary embolism) as a possible contributor to the pulmonary embolism; other risk factors included a history of varicose veins of the lower limbs, rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension and smoking. No other embolic or thrombotic events occurred in either study. Herpes zoster occurred in two patients in each treatment group in STOP-V1 and in one patient in the povorcitinib group in STOP-V2; all were grade 2, nonserious and resolved or were resolving. There were no occurrences of gastrointestinal perforation in patients who received povorcitinib. Hypersensitivity reactions occurred in two patients in each treatment group in STOP-V1 and in one patient in the placebo group in STOP-V2; all were grade 1 or 2, and none were considered related to treatment. There were no clinically meaningful trends in liver (alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b) or hematology parameters (hemoglobin, platelets) (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b) associated with povorcitinib and no indicators of drug-induced liver injury. No trends regarding weight gain were observed in either study. Visible, progressive repigmentation of both facial (Fig. 4a,b) and body (Fig. 4c,d) lesions was observed in different patients who received povorcitinib. Continued improvement in the mean percentage change from baseline in F-VASI was observed with povorcitinib versus placebo to week 52 in both studies (STOP-V1, −36.8% versus −10.1%; STOP-V2, −36.4% versus −8.3%) (Extended Data Fig. 6), with separation between treatment groups observed from week 12 onward. a–d, Selected clinical images of facial repigmentation (a,b) and body repigmentation (c,d) in different patients treated with povorcitinib. Sensitivity and supplementary analyses of the primary endpoint, including NRI, multiple imputation, longitudinal logistic regression and analysis of the per-protocol population, were consistent with the primary analysis in both studies (Extended Data Table 3). In addition, F-VASI75 response rates at week 52 were generally consistent across prespecified subgroups, including age, sex, race and baseline disease characteristics (Extended Data Fig. 7). Post hoc analyses indicated increased disease stabilization with povorcitinib treatment. In both studies, a higher proportion of patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo had no increase in T-VASI (suggesting no worsening or progression of disease) at week 52 (STOP-V1, 94.3% versus 71.8%; STOP-V2, 87.6% versus 69.2%); comparable results were observed among patients with active disease at baseline (STOP-V1, 95.5% versus 73.4%; STOP-V2, 84.2% versus 66.7%). Similarly, more patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo had no new lesions and no expansion of existing lesions at week 52 in the overall study populations (STOP-V1, 94.2% versus 80.3%; STOP-V2, 84.2% versus 78.7%) and among patients with active disease at baseline (STOP-V1, 92.4% versus 79.7%; STOP-V2, 75.4% versus 72.5%). There is substantial unmet need for systemic repigmentation therapies among patients with moderate-to-severe vitiligo. The INTERCEPT consensus identified affected BSA as the starting point for assessment of vitiligo severity (mild, <3%; moderate, 3% to <10%; severe, ≥10%)12. Additional factors, including disease activity, involvement of highly visible areas (for example, the face and hands) and psychosocial burden (for example, stigmatization) may escalate patients from moderate to severe disease; rapidly progressing or spreading disease is considered severe regardless of BSA involvement12. Consistent with the INTERCEPT consensus, the STOP-V studies enrolled systemic-eligible adults with moderate-to-severe NSV. In the STOP-V studies, povorcitinib 30 mg QD demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements versus placebo in facial and total body repigmentation over 52 weeks. The primary and key secondary endpoints of F-VASI75 and T-VASI50, both of which had significantly higher response rates with povorcitinib versus placebo, represent thresholds of meaningful change among both patients and clinicians26,27. F-VASI75 response rates were consistent across prespecified subgroups for demographics (for example, race and skin type) and baseline disease characteristics (for example, disease duration). In addition, the proportions of patients achieving facial VNS 4 or 5 with povorcitinib in each study were approaching the proportions achieving F-VASI75, indicating that patient-perceived improvements align with measured clinical improvements. There was a consistently higher placebo response rate across endpoints in STOP-V1 versus STOP-V2. Although the reason for this is unknown, patients in STOP-V2 having more extensive disease at baseline versus those in STOP-V1 may have contributed to a lower placebo response. In addition, assessment of depigmentation may be more difficult in patients with skin types I and II (STOP-V1, 42%; STOP-V2, 32%), and STOP-V1 included more study sites versus STOP-V2 (81 versus 68) with approximately the same number of total patients; both factors may contribute to overall variability. Discontinuation rates in the STOP-V studies were low (17–18%) and comparable between treatment groups despite 1-year placebo control without rescue for potentially worsening patients. Repigmentation with povorcitinib increased to week 52 without evidence of plateau across efficacy endpoints, suggesting that further improvement may occur with continued treatment. This trajectory is consistent with the biology of repigmentation in vitiligo, which often requires prolonged, continuous treatment13,28. Accordingly, longer treatment duration is likely needed to achieve increased T-VASI75 response rates (a stringent threshold for repigmentation), which were low at week 52 in both studies. The use of UVB phototherapy in combination with povorcitinib may further improve or accelerate repigmentation, as previously demonstrated with other topical and oral JAK inhibitors29,30. Patients enrolled in the STOP-V studies had extensive disease (mean baseline T-VASI ~20), most had long-standing disease (>10 years) and approximately one-third of patients in both studies had physical signs of active disease at baseline, including confetti pigmentation, Koebner phenomenon and trichrome appearance of vitiligo. Active disease is associated with increased psychosocial and quality-of-life burden8,10. In addition to repigmentation, disease stabilization may be a meaningful treatment goal for patients with active disease28,31. In both STOP-V studies, a higher proportion of patients who received povorcitinib versus placebo had no increase in T-VASI as well as no new lesions or expansion of existing lesions at week 52, suggesting a possible effect on disease progression. Between both studies, patients from three continents (North America, Europe and Asia) were included. Patients with all Fitzpatrick skin types were included in both studies, with most patients having skin types II, III or IV. In addition, a substantial proportion of patients in both studies had vitiligo affecting anatomic regions generally considered refractory to treatment, including the hands, feet and genitals. Povorcitinib 30 mg QD was well tolerated, with no new safety signals identified; results were consistent with its known safety profile23,32,33. The overall rates of TEAEs were similar between povorcitinib and placebo treatment groups and across both studies (63–69%). The rates of serious TEAEs were low and similar between the povorcitinib and placebo groups. The most common grade ≥3 TEAE was increased blood CPK; none were serious, and most of these events were attributed to intense physical activity, consistent with an exertional rather than a drug-mediated mechanism. Dose-dependent increases in blood CPK are a recognized, generally asymptomatic effect of systemic JAK inhibition34,35,36 and are not typically associated with clinical events37. The lack of clinically meaningful trends in liver or hematology parameters associated with povorcitinib treatment supports its overall laboratory safety profile and may suggest that continuous laboratory monitoring is not needed. In addition, JAK inhibitor class-specific TEAEs were infrequent or absent, with no MACE, tuberculosis or mortality in either study. Basal cell carcinoma (an NMSC) occurred in four patients who received povorcitinib; all were grade 1 or 2 and resolved, and several patients had prior phototherapy or a history of skin cancer. NMSCs of mild or moderate severity have been reported in other vitiligo studies with topical or systemic JAK inhibitors38,39. Thromboembolic events occurred in a single patient with several established risk factors; this low incidence is consistent with the thromboembolic safety profile reported with other oral JAK inhibitors40. Several other oral JAK inhibitors are currently being evaluated in patients with vitiligo38,41,42,43. Interferon-gamma signaling, a key mediator in vitiligo pathogenesis14, requires JAK1 and JAK2. Because JAK2 is essential for hematopoiesis44, selective targeting of JAK1 may reduce cytopenias associated with less-selective JAK inhibition. Povorcitinib demonstrated potent selectivity for JAK1 while sparing JAK2, had no activity against JAK3 and had negligible potency toward tyrosine kinase 222. At the highest povorcitinib clinical dose evaluated (75 mg QD), model-informed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses indicated sustained JAK1 inhibition with minimal JAK2 engagement25, supporting a wide margin between the therapeutic dose and doses at which JAK2-related safety concerns would be expected. Consistent with this JAK1-selective mechanism, povorcitinib 30 mg QD treatment resulted in no clinically meaningful changes in hematology parameters (hemoglobin, platelets) over 52 weeks in the STOP-V studies. The overall safety profile of povorcitinib was generally consistent with long-term data reported with oral JAK1 inhibitors in other dermatological conditions45. Weight gain, as has been noted with other oral JAK inhibitors45,46, was not observed in the STOP-V studies. Further analysis of weight gain in patients with vitiligo treated with oral JAK inhibitors may be warranted, because different inflammatory conditions could independently contribute to metabolic abnormalities. The STOP-V studies were placebo-controlled without an active comparator, precluding direct comparisons with other therapies. Cross-trial comparisons are further limited by substantial differences in study populations, study design and other methodological factors (both disease-specific and independent). Additional limitations of the STOP-V studies include eligibility criteria that may not fully reflect a real-world comorbid population. Povorcitinib was assessed as a monotherapy, whereas many clinicians typically use combination therapy approaches in practice. Furthermore, the high percentage of white patients (80–85%) may limit generalizability to the global population. Study data are limited to the 52-week placebo-controlled period, and longer treatment duration is likely needed to fully assess the maximal treatment effect, because repigmentation is a slow process; however, the upward trend in repigmentation over 1 year is promising and consistent with other clinical trial data42,47,48. The 52-week open-label extension is ongoing and will provide additional long-term efficacy and safety data. In summary, povorcitinib treatment provided clinically meaningful repigmentation for adult patients with NSV (per F-VASI75 and T-VASI50 outcomes) and showed continued improvement in efficacy outcomes over 1 year without plateau. The risk–benefit profile of povorcitinib 30 mg QD was favorable, with no new safety signals identified. These 52-week findings from the STOP-V studies demonstrate that povorcitinib is an effective and well-tolerated systemic treatment option for adults with moderate-to-severe NSV. No information was collected regarding gender. Patients were randomized 1:1 using an interactive response technology to receive oral povorcitinib 30 mg or placebo QD for 52 weeks. The current analysis reports the 52-week primary results from both STOP-V studies. The primary endpoint of the STOP-V studies was the proportion of patients achieving ≥75% improvement from baseline in F-VASI (F-VASI75) at week 52. Key secondary endpoints were the proportion of patients achieving a facial VNS score of 4 (a lot less noticeable) or 5 (no longer noticeable) at week 52, the proportion of patients achieving ≥50% improvement from baseline in T-VASI (T-VASI50) at week 52, the proportion of patients achieving ≥75% improvement from baseline in T-VASI (T-VASI75) at week 52 and the percentage change from baseline in T-VASI at week 52. Other secondary efficacy endpoints were achievement of ≥50% improvement from baseline in F-VASI (F-VASI50), ≥90% improvement from baseline in F-VASI (F-VASI90), ≥90% improvement from baseline in T-VASI (T-VASI90), FsIGA and sIGA of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear), and F-PaGIC-V and T-PaGIC-V, respectively of ‘very much improved’ or ‘much improved’ at week 52; the proportion of patients in each category of the FsIGA, sIGA, F-PaGIC-V, T-PaGIC-V, and a color-matching question where patients rated color match between facial treated vitiligo skin and normal skin from 1 (excellent) to 5 (very poor) at week 52; and the change from baseline in VitiQoL and HADS at week 52. The percentage change from baseline in F-VASI was assessed as an exploratory endpoint. The proportion of patients with no increase in T-VASI and the proportion of patients with no new or expanding lesions were assessed in post hoc analyses. Safety and tolerability were assessed through the frequency and severity of TEAEs (coded by the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 27.1 and the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0) and clinical laboratory parameters. TEAEs of special interest included MACE and thrombotic events, malignancy, serious infections (defined as any infection meeting the protocol-defined criteria for serious adverse events), opportunistic infections (including herpes zoster and tuberculosis), gastrointestinal perforations and hypersensitivity reactions. The VASI is a composite measure of both affected BSA and degree of depigmentation on the face (F-VASI; range, 0–3) or total body (T-VASI; range, 0–100)49. F-BSA considers depigmented areas on the face, excluding the ears, lips, neck and scalp. T-BSA considers depigmented areas on all body regions, including the face, head and/or neck, upper extremities, hands, trunk, lower extremities and feet. The VNS is a patient-reported measure of vitiligo treatment success50. Patients assessed current vitiligo on their face using a mirror and reported noticeability compared to a baseline facial photograph on a scale from 1 (more noticeable) to 5 (no longer noticeable), with a score of 4 or 5 representing treatment success. The FsIGA and sIGA are global measures of vitiligo severity from 0 (clear) to 5 (severe) that incorporate location, distribution, size, depigmentation and signs of activity. The F-PaGIC-V and T-PaGIC-V are patient-reported assessments of vitiligo improvement from 1 (very much improved) to 7 (very much worse). For the facial color-matching question, patients were provided with a mirror and asked to rate the facial color match between treated vitiligo skin and normal skin from 1 (excellent) to 5 (very poor); patients were shown their baseline facial image for reference. The VitiQoL is a 15-item patient-reported quality-of-life assessment in which various aspects of the condition are rated on a 7-point scale from ‘not at all’ to ‘all of the time’51. The HADS is a 14-item questionnaire assessing anxiety and depression (7 questions each, scored from 0 to 3; higher scores indicate more severe anxiety and depression)52. Based on results from the phase 2 dose-ranging study using nonresponder imputation (povorcitinib) and the linear extrapolation method (placebo), assumed F-VASI75 response rates for the povorcitinib 30 mg and placebo groups were 20% and 8%, respectively. Sample size calculations using the χ2square test (two-sided α = 0.05) and an assumed 30% dropout rate determined that approximately 444 patients per study would provide 95.6% power to detect a difference between povorcitinib 30 mg and placebo in the primary endpoint of F-VASI75. The assumed response rates for the key secondary endpoints were as follows: percentage change in T-VASI, −35% for povorcitinib 30 mg and −5% for placebo; T-VASI50, 15% and 5%; VNS 4 or 5, 12% and 4%; T-VASI75, 7% and 2%; the corresponding estimated powers for the key secondary endpoints were >99.9%, 94.2%, 87.7% and 72.1%, respectively. The intent-to-treat population, used for all efficacy analyses, included all randomized patients. The safety population included all patients who received ≥1 dose of study drug. To support the robustness of the primary analysis, three sensitivity analyses (nonresponder imputation, multiple imputation, longitudinal logistic regression) and one supportive analysis (of the per-protocol population (all randomized patients considered to be sufficiently compliant with the protocol)) were also conducted. Primary and key secondary endpoints were tested using a gatekeeping approach in a fixed sequence (F-VASI75, percentage change from baseline in T-VASI, T-VASI50, VNS 4 or 5, T-VASI75 (all at week 52)) to control the rate of overall family-wise type I error with a two-sided α of 0.05. Statistical significance for the primary and binary key secondary endpoints was assessed using the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test with stratification for F-VASI (<1.5 and ≥1.5), T-VASI (4–20 and >20) and Fitzpatrick skin type (I–II and III–VI). The common OR and corresponding 95% CI for the comparison between treatment groups are reported. The percentage change in T-VASI was analyzed using an analysis of covariance model with treatment group and stratification factors as the fixed factors, and baseline T-VASI as covariates. The LSM treatment difference, associated 95% CI and P value are reported. Patients with missing data at week 52 for the primary endpoint and key secondary endpoints with binary outcomes were imputed using mNRI. The use of mNRI was expected to better represent actual response rates in comparison to NRI. Patients who initiated prohibited therapy with potential impact on vitiligo outcomes before week 52 were considered nonresponders for all subsequent visits after the date of the intercurrent event. Patients with missing data for any other reason were imputed using multiple imputation (fully conditional specification method with treatment group, stratification factors and baseline and postbaseline scores as predictors). For percentage change from baseline in T-VASI, patients who initiated prohibited therapy with potential impact on vitiligo outcomes before week 52 were imputed using the baseline T-VASI score. Patients with missing data at week 52 were imputed using multiple imputation; missing data were imputed similar to binary outcomes followed by an analysis using the analysis of covariance model with treatment group, stratification factors and corresponding baseline values as predictors. By-visit analyses and all other endpoints are reported as observed and summarized using descriptive statistics. SAS software (SAS Institute Inc.; v9.1 or later) was used for all statistical analyses. title: When and where to watch FC Barcelona v Aston Villa - Official FC Barcelona Website
content: After getting back to winning ways in La Liga with an emphatic victory over Alavés, Barça now turn their attention to the Champions League, where they will be looking to claim another three points. Standing in their way are Aston Villa, one of just five teams to have won all three of their opening games in the competition, while the blaugranes have taken six points from a possible nine. As always, fans around the world can follow the action via the Club website's live match centre, the official app and Barça Live, available on Barça Play and the club's YouTube channel. Updates will also be available on the Club's official social media channels. Below is a guide to kick-off times around the world. Please note that local kick-off times in many countries have changed since the match against PSG due to the recent changes to summer and winter time.
